Simulation studies and a coating degradation application demonstrate the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed methods.

title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis
abstract: Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players' service performance, and a Bradley--Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set's number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men's matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women's tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings
abstract: The design and evaluation of public health interventions in humanitarian crises demand rigorous yet flexible methodological approaches. Cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) are increasingly used to generate evidence in such settings, but trial conduct is frequently complicated by displacement, resource constraints, and cluster dropout. Although Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for hierarchical modeling, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and the integration of prior knowledge, their use in cRCT design remains limited, particularly with respect to anticipating missingness. This paper introduces a Bayesian design strategy tailored for cRCTs in complex settings, motivated by a forthcoming trial in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, that will assess a community health worker adherence intervention for cardiovascular disease and hepatitis C. Our approach incorporates prior information on cluster and individual-level dropout into power and sample size calculations via a hierarchical model and push-forward distribution framework. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method under varying levels of missingness and correlation structures. The approach is then applied to inform the design of the Bangladesh trial. We disseminate our methods via a publicly-available R Shiny app to promote accessibility and usability to investigators. By formalizing Bayesian strategies that anticipate data loss, this work provides a foundation for more robust and efficient cRCTs in humanitarian contexts; therefore, strengthening the evidence base for health interventions in resource-limited and crisis-affected populations.

title: GeoMix: A Bayesian Framework for Stratigraphic and Geotechnical Inference
abstract: Accurate characterisation of subsea sediments is essential for engineering projects such as offshore wind farms, but the challenging environment and large spatial domains involved make dense geotechnical measurements impractical. Seismic traces offer a cheap, abundant complement, yet their geotechnical interpretation relies on subjective judgement, leading to biased, hard-to-validate predictions of sediment structure. To address this, we introduce GeoMix, a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework for jointly inferring geological stratigraphy and geotechnical properties from seismic and geotechnical data. GeoMix uses a Potts Markov random field to represent spatially coherent geology organised into distinct stratigraphic layers. Labels derived from seismic interpretation are linked to the latent stratigraphy through an observation model that captures elevated uncertainty near transitions between strata. Conditional on the latent stratigraphy, geotechnical properties are modelled using class-specific Gaussian processes, with scalable likelihood evaluation enabled by a grouped Vecchia approximation. Together, these components yield a unified latent-variable model capable of recovering stratigraphy, quantifying uncertainty, and predicting geotechnical properties across large three-dimensional domains. Simulation studies and an application to the IJmuiden Ver offshore wind farm show that GeoMix produces spatially coherent stratigraphic estimates and sediment predictions that are better calibrated and more accurate than existing approaches.

title: Testing Tail-Index Homogeneity via Exceedance-Covariate Independence
abstract: We propose a test of whether the tail index of a heavy-tailed outcome is homogeneous across observed covariates. The key observation is that, under tail-index homogeneity, normalized log exceedances are asymptotically independent of the covariates even when tail frequencies vary with them. This leads to a simple-to-implement permutation test based on distance covariance, without estimating conditional tail indices or specifying the form of tail-index heterogeneity. For the global and locally balanced versions, we establish validity for order-statistic thresholds and give conditions for consistency and local power. Local balancing selects extremes within two covariate groups and can improve power when tail selection concentrates the covariates. Simulations illustrate these gains. In French motor insurance data, upper conditional quantiles vary with risk characteristics, but the tail-index tests do not reject a common tail index.

title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
abstract: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

title: Are continuous models better than areal models for spatial disease mapping with a large number of small areas?
authors: Sara Martino and Mar\'ia Dolores Ugarte
abstract: Classical methods for analysing areal mortality data typically rely on Poisson mixed models, which account for spatial and unstructured variability through prior distributions such as the BYM2 prior. This paper investigates alternative modeling approaches for settings involving a large number of small areas. Specifically, we explore the Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE) approach for continuous risk surfaces, examining an existing model from the literature alongside a proposed modification that incorporates an unstructured random effect. Finally, we evaluate the performance of both hierarchical mixed Poisson models and SPDE-based frameworks through a comprehensive simulation study across various spatial configurations and aggregation levels. Furthermore, we apply these approaches to the analysis of lung cancer mortality among men and women across Spanish municipalities during the period 2009--2022.

title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
abstract: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.

title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection
abstract: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework is proposed for quickest change detection (QCD) where there are multiple experts, and each expert produces a sequence of statistics for change detection. A change is declared when a weighted sum of these statistics crosses a threshold. This framework is then applied to the problem of multi-stream QCD to obtain a family of powerful algorithms that outperform the best known algorithms in the literature. In the multi-stream QCD problem, a decision-maker observes multiple streams of observations. At the change point, the distribution of an unknown subset of the streams changes. The optimal algorithm based on a generalized likelihood ratio is computationally expensive. One of the most computationally and performance-efficient algorithms in the literature is the rank-weighted sum (RWS) scheme based on Shiryaev-Roberts statistics. It is shown in the paper that the MoE-based QCD algorithm for multi-stream data outperforms the RWS scheme. This is demonstrated through simulation results on real-valued Gaussian mean shift data and high-dimensional data from Gaussian--Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GB-RBMs).

title: Calibrated Bayesian inference for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects in stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials
abstract: Stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials (SW-CRTs) randomly assign clusters to sequences that determine when each cluster switches from control to intervention. Conventional Bayesian analyses of SW-CRTs report treatment effect coefficients from a working outcome model, but under model misspecification or informative cluster-period sizes, such coefficients can lack a clear causal interpretation. In this work, we develop Bayesian methods targeting weighted average treatment effect estimands in SW-CRTs, including novel subgroup-specific causal estimands defined by baseline characteristics. We compare model-based g-computation with model-robust standardization, implementing both with linear mixed models and mixed-effects Bayesian additive regression trees as working outcome models, and propose a calibrated variance estimator that augments posterior parameter uncertainty with cluster-level resampling to better capture sampling variability. In simulations with outcome model misspecification and informative cluster-period sizes, model-robust standardization with calibrated inference exhibits negligible bias and near-nominal frequentist coverage for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects, whereas g-computation and uncalibrated intervals become insufficient. We illustrate the proposed methods with a reanalysis of the Trauma Survivors Outcomes and Support trial.

title: Challenges and Opportunities in Statistical Analyses and Designs for Neuroscience Clinical Trials
abstract: Drug development is a complex, costly, and high-risk process, with neuroscience representing one of the most challenging therapeutic areas due to the complexity of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders. Neuroscience clinical trials face unique barriers, making the adoption of innovative statistical methods in study design, execution, and analysis especially critical for improving clarity, feasibility, efficiency, and validity in the drug development process. The ASA Biopharmaceutical Section Neuroscience Scientific Working Group (SWG) was formed to advance statistical research and address these distinct challenges. This landscape paper provides an overview of key challenges and opportunities in statistical methods and trial designs for neuroscience, offering insights to guide future research and practice in this evolving field.

title: A Geometric Framework for the Bayesian Estimation of Joint Environmental Extremes
abstract: Multivariate extreme events tend to have broader impacts on society compared to individual extremes. Flexible and accurate modeling of multivariate extremes is therefore crucial for many practical applications, including risk assessments and mitigation projects. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian modeling framework for bivariate extremes. Our approach utilizes the geometric extremes framework, for which data are decomposed into angular and radial components. The angular distribution is estimated using periodic M-splines, resulting in a natural circular density, while the radial distribution, conditional on the angles, is approximated using Bezier splines. The radial distribution also provides a means of estimating the limit set, the limiting shape of scaled sample clouds that encodes information pertaining to extremal dependence. Our Bayesian approach offers advantages over competing methods, particularly for uncertainty quantification and interpretation. Furthermore, our framework guarantees theoretical properties of limit sets, ensuring validity for inference. Notably, our model can be used to approximate extreme probabilities associated with failure sets in the joint tail, which are useful across many applications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments and a case study on fire weather in Louisiana, USA, with diagnostics for the latter indicating strong model performance.

title: Precise Asymptotics for Dense High-Dimensional Huber Regression under Heteroscedasticity
abstract: We study Huber regression in a heteroscedastic linear model in the proportional regime $n/p \to \delta \in (1, \infty)$. Our main result is an exact characterization of the asymptotic empirical distribution of the Huber estimator. This characterization is in terms of three scalar parameters which determine the first-order centre and the asymptotic variance of the Huber estimator. The result shows that with heteroscedastic noise, the first-order centre may contain an additional component along the variance index coefficient. We derive the displacement coefficients that determine this centre, as well as the exact asymptotic variance. The analysis uses the matrix approximate message passing (AMP) framework to jointly track the regression and variance index coefficients, extending the existing framework for homoscedastic M-estimators. We illustrate the implications of this characterization by constructing a test for centre displacement and examining its empirical size and power through simulations.

title: The Reach of Treatment Effects: Randomization Inference for Zero-Effect Regions
abstract: A treatment may affect some individuals while leaving others unaffected. We study the reach of treatment effects by asking how large an unaffected covariate region could be. We develop efficient local randomization tests over nearest-neighbour regions to construct a finite-sample valid upper confidence bound for the size of the largest zero-effect region. A small bound provides evidence that treatment effects extend broadly across covariate values by ruling out large zero-effect regions. Under a general outcome model, we characterize how the size of the bound depends on the number of affected units, the size of their treatment effects, and the geometry of the true zero-effect set. We show that, when region size is measured as a sample fraction, the excess of the upper confidence bound over the true size decreases to zero at a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor. Numerical simulations assess the coverage, power and computational efficiency of our method. Applications to voter-turnout, HIV clinical-trial, and AI-assisted writing data illustrate how our method rules out large zero-effect regions across the covariates of interest.

title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
authors: Luka Todorovic and Kaushal Gianchandani and Sai Ravela
abstract: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes
abstract: AI weather prediction (AIWP) models have emerged as a key complement to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, and now often outperform them on aggregate skill. Yet, several studies report that physics-based models still forecast extreme events better, in particular record-breaking extremes, based on the evaluation of deterministic forecasts. Here we evaluate heat extreme forecasts from probabilistic AIWP models over global land and show that they clearly outperform the ECMWF IFS ensemble, both raw and post-processed, including for record-breaking events, in all regions and at all lead times considered. AIWP models better forecast the occurrence and intensity of extremes, are better calibrated in the tail and miss fewer records. Station observations confirm these results. We argue that many reported AIWP limitations stem from unsuitable verification choices, specifically comparing deterministic forecasts that target different quantities. Instead, a fair evaluation of extremes necessitates probabilistic verification.

title: SafeAdapt-Poker: Counterfactual Risk Calibration for Budgeted Adaptation under Opponent Shift
abstract: Opponent histories can mislead after behavioral shifts. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of -0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.

title: What Does Disagreement Mean? A Semantic Identifiability Frontier for Pairwise Preference Learning
abstract: Pairwise comparison data are a standard supervision signal in preference learning, but disagreement in such data can reflect stable latent heterogeneity, ephemeral stochasticity, or non-binary responses hidden by a forced-choice interface. We study which of these semantic distinctions are identifiable from the feedback channel itself. We introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three querywise quantities: aggregate directional preference $\mu_q$, persistent disagreement $\tau_q$, and non-binary mass $\alpha_q$. Under the anonymous binary channel, we prove an exact semantic fiber theorem: $\mu_q$ is point-identified, whereas $(\tau_q, \alpha_q)$ vary over an explicit feasible region compatible with the same binary law. Same-annotator repeats identify $\tau_q$ through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies $\alpha_q$ directly, and together they point-identify the full semantic triple. We also derive finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, and validate the theory on theorem-matched synthetic data.

title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models
abstract: Conditional distribution equality testing is a core problem with applications in causal inference, model diagnostics, and transfer learning. Existing methods often lose power when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. We propose a new test that leverages generative models to compare conditional distributions using both observed data and synthetic samples. A sample-splitting and studentization scheme is introduced to control estimation error. Under the null, the test statistic is asymptotically normal, and we establish local power against contiguous alternatives. Our theory under the null and fixed alternative requires only consistency of the learned conditional distribution, allowing for a broad class of generative models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate size control and strong power in high-dimensional settings compared to representative kernel-based conditional and joint two-sample tests.

title: Revealing Structured Heterogeneity
abstract: In this paper, we study models of restricted heterogeneity. While the random utility model allows for arbitrary heterogeneity among rational types, we consider the case when an analyst ex-ante restricts the set of rational types to some smaller set of allowable types. We study the behavioral content, the model fit, and the identification properties of restrictions of this form. We find that all three of these can be connected through a common value function that is constructed from observable data. Consistency with a model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by this value function achieving a value of one, while model fit is given by a value that is potentially less than one. The partially identified set for a given model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by way of the subdifferential of this value function.

title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing
abstract: Standard competition-based multiple testing methods -- such as the knockoff filter and the target-decoy procedure -- are typically formulated as head-to-head competitions between a test unit and its assigned negative control unit. Motivated by real-world applications, which leverage any available negative controls, we study this competition-based framework in more intricate settings where competitions vary in size and structure. We propose new methods based on compound p-values -- p-values that are superuniform only on aggregate -- that enable powerful multiple testing with broader competition structures, via the Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures. The former provides exact familywise error rate control, whereas the latter may incur a false discovery rate inflation factor, for which we derive upper bounds across a range of settings. We showcase the performance of our general competition-based testing methodology through extensive simulations and real-data applications, including analyses of virtual spatial transcriptomics and CRISPR screen datasets that exhibit precisely the complex competition structures that motivate our methods.

title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations
abstract: Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.

title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
abstract: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.

title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model
abstract: Technological progress can give rise to new loss exposures or reduce existing risks. In either case, it strongly affects insurance companies' existing lines of business. As the magnitude of such effects is often closely connected to the innovation's market penetration, reliably predicting its adoption process is vital in enabling insurers to adapt their business strategy accordingly. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel combination of contributions from the domain of innovation diffusion. Our methodology generates adoption scenarios that holistically account for different sources of uncertainty, offers a structured way to incorporate expert judgment and insights from pre-existing technologies, and updates its predictions as new information on the technology's diffusion becomes available. Its modular nature ensures that components can be easily replaced by suitable alternatives. Using publicly accessible data on privately-owned battery electric vehicles in Germany, the application of our approach for predicting changes to insurance losses and for supporting insurers' sustainability strategies is visualized in a motor insurance case study.

title: Discrete p-Fold Directional Models for Binned Orientation Data with Applications to Sand-Grain Orientations and Urban Street Networks
abstract: Discrete directional data exhibiting p-fold rotational symmetry, where directions separated by integer multiples of 2{\pi}/p are equivalent, arise in various applications but are often modeled using continuous distributions. In this article, we develop two general methods for constructing distributions for such data: symmetrization and folding of discrete circular distributions, and wrapping of discrete linear distributions. Particular models arising from these constructions are studied, together with their properties and estimation methods. For axial sand-grain orientation data, the proposed models are compared with discretized continuous axial distributions, whose category probabilities require numerical integration. The proposed models attain smaller Akaike information criterion values among the models considered while allowing direct likelihood evaluation without numerical integration. The framework is also applied to binned Manhattan street-orientation data, demonstrating its applicability to higher-order rotational structures, specifically the 4-fold case.

title: No-Regret Learning in Stackelberg Security Games with an Unknown, Bounded Set of Attacker Types
abstract: In a repeated Stackelberg security game, a defender commits in every round to a randomized allocation of its resources, and an attacker, drawn from a set of types, best-responds. Existing no-regret guarantees assume that the defender knows this set of types in advance. We drop this assumption: the set of types is unknown, and its size is at most $K_{\max}$, an upper bound that the defender is not told. We show that what can be learned then depends on what the defender observes. If it observes the type of each attacker, an algorithm that adds types to its list as they appear achieves regret $\tilde O(nK_{\max}\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ rounds with $n$ targets, the same $\sqrt T$ rate as with known types, at an extra factor of only $\sqrt{K_{\max}}$ and without ever using $K_{\max}$. If it observes only the attacked target and types come from an infinite universe, no algorithm has sublinear regret: in a fixed three-target game every algorithm suffers regret at least $T-2$, even against a single attacker type, because it cannot tell which type it faces. If, in addition, it is told every $B$ rounds which types have appeared so far, sublinear regret returns, at $\tilde O(nK_{\max}^{4/3}T^{2/3}+K_{\max} B)$. The first term is the rate of the partial-information learner we use, and we show that the additive cost of the delay cannot be avoided.

title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels
abstract: We study testing for peer effects in linear panel models with individual and time fixed effects when the interaction network is unspecified. We propose a quadratic-form test based on the Gram matrix of residualized peer covariates. A key difficulty is that fixed-effects removal and nuisance estimation destroy the centering of a conventional leave-diagonal-out quadratic form under conditional heteroskedasticity. We introduce a leverage adjustment that restores exact conditional centering and combine it with a residual-based variance estimator. The resulting studentized statistic is asymptotically standard normal as both panel dimensions diverge, without imposing any restriction on their relative growth rates. Under additional conditions, we establish consistency against alternatives. The null theory is further extended to covariates that are weakly dependent over time; the same studentization remains valid without an additional long-run variance estimator. Monte Carlo experiments evaluate the finite-sample size and power of the proposed test across different settings and demonstrate its favorable performance relative to the existing benchmark test. Applications to state tax competition and growth spillovers among OECD countries illustrate the practical relevance in testing for peer effects without specifying the interaction network.

title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights
abstract: Many multivariate time series arise on networks where relationships between variables depend on physical or more general distances. Standard vector autoregressive models struggle in such settings due to their quadratic parameter growth, while generalised network autoregressive (GNAR) models offer a parsimonious alternative by explicitly incorporating network structures. Existing GNAR formulations assume fixed weights, typically uniform or reciprocal distances, which may not reflect the true influence of distance in real systems. We introduce a novel model with general inverse distance weights (GNARID) that extends GNAR by introducing a tunable exponent parameter that controls the strength of distance penalisation. We establish theoretical results on the consistency and asymptotic normality of new GNARID estimators, including an extension to the setting where the number of nodes grows. We analyse the effect of misspecifying the exponent on forecasting error, which helps assess how much GNAR models could be improved by our tunable weights. Simulation studies confirm the theoretical properties and show measurable benefits from correct weight specification. Using the Brumadinho ground displacement dataset, we show that proper tuning of the weight exponent improves predictive performance, highlighting the practical value of flexible distance-based weighting in network time series models.

title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual R\'enyi Entropy
abstract: This paper introduces a new cumulative residual R\'enyi entropy (CRRE), which addresses limitations of the existing cumulative residual R\'enyi entropy. The conventional measure suffers from two primary drawbacks: its failure to converge to the cumulative residual entropy (CRE) as the order parameter approaches unity, and its lack of guaranteed positivity. Our proposed CRRE resolves these issues, offering a theoretically consistent and always nonnegative measure of uncertainty in residual lifetimes. We explore its mathematical properties, including its relationship with existing information measures. Furthermore, the concept is extended to its dynamic version, and its time-dependent characteristics are investigated. A non-parametric estimator of the proposed CRRE is developed, its almost sure convergence is established, and is validated through Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of CRRE as a tool for quantifying uncertainty is confirmed through its application in chaotic theory and financial data.

title: Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration as a Composable Solana Primitive
abstract: Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.

title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB
authors: Marco Riani and Anthony C. Atkinson and Aldo Corbellini and Domenico Perrotta and Francesca Torti and Gianluca Morelli
abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard method for dimension reduction and the exploratory analysis of multivariate data, but a complete applied workflow often requires more than numerical eigenvectors and static plots. This article documents a set of routines in the FSDA toolbox for MATLAB that implements an integrated workflow for interactive and robust PCA graphics. The software contribution consists of coordinating classical SVD-based PCA, dynamic biplot scaling controlled by row and column parameters, score-distance and orthogonal-distance diagnostics, hard-trimming robust PCA through the Minimum Covariance Determinant and the Forward Search, linked brushing, geographical displays, and three-dimensional projection diagnostics. The implementation returns reproducible numerical output while also exposing graphical controls for changing biplot geometry, confidence regions, displayed labels, robust trimming levels, and linked selections. The methodology is illustrated on quality-of-life indicators for Italian provinces, where the software reveals variable groups, atypical provinces, robust and non-robust PCA structures, and geographical patterns. The emphasis is on statistical software: no new PCA estimator is proposed, but established PCA and robust-PCA methodology is combined in a documented, extensible, and script-reproducible MATLAB environment.

title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves
abstract: This paper develops a principal component analysis framework for probability measures associated with non-negative real-valued random variables with structural zeros. Specifically, leveraging the associated Lorenz Curve (LC) and a suitable perspective transformation of the plane, a bijective embedding is defined to treat such measures as functional data in a Hilbert space. Once the random LC is embedded in this space, standard Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) becomes directly applicable, and the diffeomorphic nature of the embedding allows the main convergence results and their interpretations to be transferred back to the original space of LC. The a.s. and $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ consistency of the estimated eigenfunctions, eigenvalues, and modes of variation is subsequently investigated, both in the embedded space and, by virtue of the embedding's diffeomorphism property, in the original LC space. Crucially, this consistency analysis accounts for the double stochasticity of the estimation problem: one level of randomness is tied to the underlying LC process itself, while the other stems from the empirical estimation of the LC from sample data. As a consequence, consistency of the Karhunen--Lo\`eve reconstructions is also established, guaranteeing faithful approximation of individual curves in both spaces. Finally, the proposed FPCA methodology is illustrated on a real-world dataset of global export flows and compared with a naive FPCA approach.

title: Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
abstract: We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss. Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching. Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.

title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates
abstract: Background: Generalized Odds (Gen Odds) provide summaries for ordinal outcomes without requiring the proportional odds assumption. However, conventional Gen Odds compares independently drawn treatment and control outcomes and targets a population-level contrast rather than an individual-level contrast. We developed an individual-level causal formulation of Gen Odds and examined its identification. Methods: We defined the Causal Gen Odds using the joint distribution of potential outcomes and identified it under conditional independence of the potential outcomes given baseline covariates. We developed a model-based estimator using nonproportional cumulative logistic regression and introduced an odds-ratio sensitivity parameter to assess departures from conditional independence. We evaluated the estimators through simulations and illustrated them using data from the ACCORD Study. Results: In simulations, the conditional-independence estimator was approximately unbiased with 95.5% confidence interval coverage under conditional independence, but bias and undercoverage increased with residual dependence. When the sensitivity-analysis estimator incorporated the data-generating dependence parameter, bias remained below 0.01 and coverage ranged from 93.7% to 96.1% across examined settings. In the ACCORD Study, the Causal Gen Odds for right-foot pre-tibial edema was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.880 to 0.940) under conditional independence and remained stable across the examined sensitivity range. Conclusions: The Causal Gen Odds provides an individual-level estimand that complements the conventional population-level Gen Odds. This framework enables estimation of this contrast while explicitly assessing its robustness to assumptions about dependence between potential outcomes.

title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
authors: Bodhayan Roy and Mohammad Azharuddin Sanpui
abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
authors: Martin Feldkircher and Bernd Prostmaier and Paul Hofmarcher and Pierre Siklos
abstract: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

title: Effective-Balance Design in Ethereum Proof-of-Stake
abstract: Proof-of-Stake (PoS) systems offer a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to Proof-of-Work (PoW). The economic security of PoS relies critically on incentivizing broad and meaningful participation through well-cali\-brated staking reward mechanisms. We study Ethe\-reum's effective-balance rules as a mechanism-design problem in which the protocol chooses a reward coefficient, an activation threshold, and a maximum effective balance, and validators respond in the induced propor\-tional-allocation game. For fixed participating validators and identity counts, we establish a unique Nash equilibrium in validator-level total stakes. When validators can split or merge their visible identities, each candidate identity structure must be evaluated after the market re-clears. Restructuring incentives therefore depend on post-reset payoff comparisons that account for all validators' stake responses. For an illustrative simulation, we construct address-level budget proxies from Beacon Chain deposits and withdrawals, Lido staking flows, Etherscan balances, and calibrated synthetic agents. With illustrative cost coefficients, lowering the reserve price from 32 ETH to 30 ETH increases active identities by 5.922\% and total effective stake by 0.098\%.

title: PPAD-Completeness of Contiguous Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Additive Valuations
authors: Bodhayan Roy and Mohammad Azharuddin Sanpui
abstract: We prove that computing a complete contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free cake allocation is PPAD-complete for normalized rational piecewise-constant additive valuations. The hardness holds even when $\varepsilon$ is given in unary, and even when every density takes only two values, which are the same for all agents, and is piecewise constant with at most six breakpoints. As a consequence, computing an exact contiguous envy-free allocation is also PPAD-complete, and the hardness holds under the same restrictions on the densities. Our key ingredient is to assign prices to the pieces so that, in every approximately envy-free allocation, all prices are nearly equal, regardless of how the pieces are assigned to the agents. We further show that, for every fixed integer $c\ge1$, computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of indivisible goods on a path is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and the hardness holds even for binary valuations in which each good is valued by exactly one agent and all agents value the same number of goods.

title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation
abstract: The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift. In such settings, the expected squared jump distance can grow rapidly, leading to numerical instability or the need for prohibitively small step-sizes. We propose the saturated unadjusted Langevin algorithm (SULA) that pairs a saturated gradient drift with a gradient-informed state-dependent diffusion, while preserving first-order consistency with the Langevin diffusion. The drift and diffusion terms are chosen to guarantee that the one-step squared update is independent of the gradient. Consequently, SULA is robust to the choice of step-size and preserves estimation and prediction quality. We provide sufficient conditions under which SULA with a step-size $h$ converges weakly to the Langevin diffusion at the standard $O(h)$ rate, the SULA chain is geometrically ergodic, and that the bias of its invariant measure relative to the target is $O(h)$. Further, we develop SG-SULA, a stochastic-gradient version of SULA that rescales the stochastic gradient using a Gaussian CDF correction under Gaussianity of the gradient noise. Numerical experiments on various examples demonstrate SULA's robustness to tuning and SG-SULA's improved predictive performance.

title: Model-Induced Hazard Geometry and Functional Representations in Survival Analysis
abstract: Individualized survival predictions are often summarized by scalar risk scores or event probabilities at selected time horizons, although clinically relevant risk may also differ in its temporal organization. We consider finite-dimensional representations of individual hazard trajectories through interpretable hazard functionals, such as peak timing, cumulative hazard over prespecified intervals, and persistence of elevated risk. A central issue is that the richness of such representations is constrained by the hazard geometry supported by the underlying survival model. We formalize this through model-induced tangent spaces and functional ranks, derive an exact decomposition of model-supported variation into directions retained and lost by a chosen representation, and introduce a model-relative notion of local completeness. We further distinguish intrinsic model capacity from the variation actually activated by covariates. These results motivate a structured extension of AFT time scaling through a positive-affine deformation on the log-time scale, yielding a power-warp mechanism with an additional temporal deformation direction. Combined with a log-logistic reference hazard, this gives a parsimonious likelihood-based working specification for which peak timing and peak height provide complete coordinates over the unimodal regime. We also establish plug-in recovery and asymptotic inference for hazard functionals. Simulations and a lung-cancer application illustrate how model-induced restrictions propagate to hazard-functional representations.

title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
abstract: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.

title: Building a Sovereign Benchmark The Limits of Private Coordination
abstract: Public debt supplies liquidity and collateral services only if institutions coordinate on using the same claim. We study this coordination when use carries a recurring cost and a benefit that rises with other users. Above a quality threshold, two positive-adoption equilibria exist, and under best responses the initial user base decides between collapse and high adoption. Under logit choice, as the population grows and noise vanishes, the long-run distribution selects high adoption only above a strictly higher threshold. Debt issuance improves market depth but eventually dilutes backing per claim. This trade-off creates a range of debt levels supporting the liquidity premium of public debt in macroeconomic models and a narrower range supporting its long-run selection. At the boundary of the wider range, the premium is discontinuous. A matching transfer that corrects the adoption externality makes stationary selection maximize network surplus. Transfers can also help launch a network without permanent support.

title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
abstract: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

title: Who Keeps a Bubble Alive? Skin in the Game and the Survival of Rational Bubbles
abstract: We study how retained ownership supports the value of an asset that pays no dividends and is held only for resale. A sponsor chooses hidden maintenance that determines market survival, bears its full cost, and captures only the benefit accruing to its retained tokens. A positive stationary equilibrium exists if and only if retention meets an endogenous minimum. Under additional curvature restrictions, retention above this threshold supports two positive stationary equilibria. Conditional on survival, prices below the upper equilibrium converge to the lower one while the upper price is the largest feasible initial valuation. Greater retention expands the feasible price interval. Credible news that future retention will be below the minimum causes an immediate collapse through backward unraveling. The model identifies a governance channel through which insider unlocks can affect valuation without changing total token supply or fundamental cash flows.

title: What You Earn from What You Learn: Characterization and Complexity of the Value of Information
abstract: We examine the value of information in extensive-form decision problems: the largest multiplicative gain that a decision maker can obtain from an information refinement, taken over all payoff environments. This measures the structural importance of information disentangled from any particular payoff specification, and generalizes the notion of value of recall recently introduced by Berker et al. (AAAI'25). We establish a unifying characterization of the value of information under any information refinement, uncovering an intriguing connection to the maximum fractional chromatic number over a certain family of conflict graphs. We then employ our characterization to elucidate the complexity of two central information refinements. First, for the value of perfect information in perfect-recall decision problems, we find that the relevant conflict graphs are cographs, so the fractional chromatic number collapses to the clique number. Even though the clique number is tractable for a given cograph, we show that the additional layer of optimization (over the family of graphs) makes computing the value of perfect information NP-complete. On the positive side, we prove fixed-parameter tractability in terms of the degree of imperfect information. Second, for the value of recall in imperfect-recall decision problems (with no absentmindedness), we first show that the value of recall can realize the fractional chromatic number of any graph. Interestingly, this implies that, unlike the value of perfect information, the value of recall can take fractional values. Building on this reduction, we then establish S2P-completeness. This addresses questions left open by Berker et al. (AAAI'25)---both on the characterization and the complexity of the value of recall---and shows that computing the value of recall is strictly harder than the value of perfect information.

title: Common Signals, Spurious Cross-Excitation, and Identification in Multivariate Hawkes Processes
abstract: Multivariate Hawkes models are widely used to measure endogenous interactions in event data, but latent common signals can generate apparent excitation even without structural interaction. We characterize the resulting linear projection and construct stable, nonnegative Hawkes processes that share the mean intensity and Bartlett spectrum of common-signal models despite having different excitation mechanisms. This establishes a concrete form of second-order non-identification. We derive integrated third-order cumulants for Hawkes processes with Cox immigration and establish generic local identification of normalized structural parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems. An exact-equivalence Monte Carlo experiment demonstrates how third-order information can distinguish mechanisms with identical second-order structure, while revealing substantial finite-sample limitations under weak signals. For a restricted parametric family, we develop Whittle estimation from binned counts, establish consistency and asymptotic normality under appropriate identification conditions, and construct feasible sandwich standard errors accounting for estimated mean intensities. Simulations assess structural recovery and inference accuracy. An application to cryptocurrency transactions illustrates the sensitivity of inferred excitation to model specification and the limitations of structural interpretation based on spectral fit alone.

title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators
abstract: Functional brain aging is often characterized by differences between people of different ages, although aging unfolds within individuals. This distinction is especially important for functional connectivity, where the direction of covariance change may evolve across adulthood. We introduce a Bayesian longitudinal covariance-operator framework that models each visit covariance as a latent positive-definite state informed by repeated resting-state fMRI runs. The approach calibrates run-level information for temporal dependence and replicate variability, separates within-person aging from between-person age differences, and uses an adaptive tangent representation to learn the low-dimensional structure of longitudinal change without relying on pooled covariance variation. The longitudinal operator varies smoothly in magnitude and orientation with age, while exact Fr\'echet derivatives translate the fitted trajectory to the covariance scale. This framework allows us to examine how brain covariance organization changes within individuals, whether longitudinal aging follows the population age gradient, and which functional systems contribute to their divergence. In the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, within-person covariance aging differs substantially from the cross-sectional age gradient through early and middle adulthood, with the discrepancy diminishing later in life. Covariance reorganization is strongest around midlife, and the longitudinal signal is concentrated in a few coordinated directions, with most off-diagonal change occurring between functional systems. These findings demonstrate that population-level signatures of brain aging do not necessarily reflect individual aging trajectories and highlight the importance of modeling longitudinal covariance change directly.

title: Subdata Selection for Measurement-Constrained Linear Regression under Model Misspecification
authors: Yundi Kong and Min Yang and Ping-Shou Zhong
abstract: In many modern applications, obtaining response variables is costly, time-consuming, or technically challenging, making it impractical to measure outcomes for all available units. In such settings, covariates may be available for a large pool of candidates, but responses can only be collected for a small, carefully selected subset, making the choice of which units to measure a consequential decision. Most existing subsampling methods are developed for massive datasets, emphasizing the trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost, and typically relying on the assumption of a correctly specified model. These features limit their suitability in measurement-constrained settings, where statistical efficiency is paramount and model misspecification is often unavoidable. To address these challenges, we develop a new subset selection framework for linear regression that accommodates potential model misspecification. The proposed approach targets predictive expected loss and yields an A-optimality-type criterion that depends only on covariate information, requiring no response observations at the selection stage. We refer to this method as Expected Loss Optimal Selection (ELOS). By focusing on predictive risk rather than model-based optimality, ELOS remains well-defined and robust under misspecification. Simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate that ELOS achieves strong predictive performance and compares favorably with existing methods across a range of scenarios.

title: On Local Inference for Functionals of Ill-Posed Inverse Problems
abstract: We study inference for continuous linear functionals of solutions to ill-posed inverse problems, including Euclidean parameters arising in nonparametric instrumental variables, proximal causal inference, and shadow-variable models. Although pointwise root-$n$ inference is possible under standard conditions, we show that this need not translate into locally reliable inference. Under a model imposing only minimal regularity conditions, the target is Hellinger discontinuous when both inverse problems are ill-posed: arbitrarily small changes in the data-generating law can produce arbitrarily large changes in the target, ruling out informative locally uniform inference. Imposing a uniform bound on a minimum-norm solution restores Hellinger continuity under regularity conditions, but does not by itself ensure stable root-n inference. If, in addition, both inverse problems are ill-posed and the solution whose norm is uniformly bounded is nonunique at a law $P_0$, then under regularity conditions the target fails to be pathwise differentiable; consequently, asymptotically linear estimators exhibit nonvanishing root-$n$ bias under some local alternatives, causing Wald confidence intervals to undercover asymptotically. Under regularity conditions, pathwise differentiability is restored if the uniformly bounded solution is unique at $P_0$. It is also restored, regardless of uniqueness, under the stronger requirement that the corresponding solution satisfy a uniformly bounded $\beta$-source condition for some $\beta$>0. We relate these regimes to very weak, weak, and strong identification in instrumental variables models.

title: Truthful and Expected-Payment-Optimal Model Routing in Graph-Based Agentic Workflows
abstract: Assigning routine tasks to cheaper large language model (LLM) providers can reduce generation cost, but switching providers may require processing accumulated context again. Keeping dependent tasks with the same provider can instead reuse eligible context. Graph-based workflows therefore couple routing decisions across tasks. Independent providers may also privately know their real-time unit costs and strategically misreport them. We formulate this routing problem as a single-parameter procurement auction and propose STAR (Strategy-proof Topology-aware Agent Routing), which minimizes virtual-cost-weighted graph workloads. Its allocation rule and payments, computed by integrating workload over possible cost reports, make truthful reporting utility-maximizing regardless of other providers' reports and cover each truthful provider's execution cost. With independent cost distributions and non-decreasing virtual costs, STAR additionally minimizes the user's expected total payment to providers. Controlled synthetic experiments separate the execution-cost benefit of topology awareness from the payment benefit of virtual-cost optimization: the former grows with fan-out and transferred payload, while the latter increases gradually along the tested prior-shape heterogeneity path. A paired sensitivity study quantifies how payment savings vary with prior misspecification while strategy-proofness is preserved.

title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation
authors: Agathe Fernandes Machado and Charlotte Jamotton and Arthur Charpentier
abstract: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. We study distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score using one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry. We distinguish two complementary constructions. Conditional and sequential audits characterize joint parity through their zero sets, but their positive values do not generally decompose a fixed joint Wasserstein disparity. By contrast, full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance is the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.

title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
abstract: While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.

title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
authors: Cristian Palma Foster and Eva Tardos
abstract: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$, each at most $\lambda_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-\lambda_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i < (1-\lambda_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $\lambda_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.

title: A Sociophysics Approach to Measuring Democracy in the Decision Making of a Group: Three Indices
abstract: A group does not usually consult all its members before every decision. This paper develops a quantitative framework for measuring how widely members are consulted in decision making within a group. Two kinds of records are considered: the number of members consulted for each decision and the number of decisions in which each member is consulted. From these records, two participation indices are defined, and their equality is proved analytically. A third index measures the fraction of decisions for which at least a specified percentage of members are consulted. The distribution of consultation levels is described using a discrete maximum-entropy model from statistical physics. Tail probabilities are used to obtain bounds for the main participation index. This study examines aggregate survey data from two groups. Their observed characteristics are broadly consistent with the patterns found across the full survey. Using binomial and Poisson calculations, the future probability that all members will be consulted for a decision is examined. Inequality in consultation among members is examined through Lorenz curves, the Gini coefficient and a normalised Shannon participation measure. The member-decision structure is represented as a bipartite network. Controlled simulations show that the same overall level of consultation can have different distributions among the members. The framework measures both the overall breadth of consultation and how consultation is distributed among the members. It therefore provides a quantitative sociophysical description of one measurable aspect of democracy in decision making within a group.

title: Student Copula Markov Networks
authors: Salha Mamane and Cheikh Tidiane Seck
abstract: This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.

title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
abstract: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting.
