For data drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution, we derive the log-likelihood-ratio distribution and its cumulants under two such hypotheses. We then search over the alternative model's parameter space and use peak prominence, the height of a likelihood-profile peak above its surrounding baseline, as an operational detection statistic. Repeating this search on simulated data drawn from the null model allows us to calibrate the prominence threshold for a specified false-positive rate. We study a toy Gaussian model as well as three cosmological examples involving cosmic topology, the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and dark energy. In all these cases, detectability of a particular model depends not only on KL divergence, but also on the size of the model parameter space, the likelihood-ratio distributions, and the distance of the model from any parameter space boundaries. The relationship between KL divergence, discovery potential, and parameter estimation must therefore be calibrated for each family of models and detection statistic under consideration.

title: Implicit and explicit reparameterizations of the Folded Normal and Rice distributions
abstract: Variational inference is a flexible tool for modeling experimental data and has proven useful in crystallography. Pathwise gradient estimators provide low-variance gradients for reparameterized variational inference, but are not readily available for some distributions central to crystallography. This work derives and implements implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in \prog{PyTorch}, and compares their variance analytically and empirically. In each case the implicit estimator achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios, while the scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. For both distributions, implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger. As a practical application, French-Wilson scaling is formulated as a variational inference problem, using the folded Normal and Rice distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, respectively. Both estimators recover the exact posterior to better than $1\%$ on the amplitude, and converge at the same rate. The implementations are available in the open-source package \prog{rs-distributions}.

title: Spatial Partner Markets: Effective Competition, Scale, and Opportunity
abstract: Local partner markets differ not only in population size but in relative partner availability, the scale of opportunity, marriage timing, and population turnover. This paper develops a county-level framework for comparing these conditions across local partner markets. The empirical application focuses on unmarried women ages 25-34 and uses observed partner-age pairings to construct age-specific weights for the relevant unmarried male population. We model absolute opportunity separately, fitting a Michaelis-Menten diminishing-returns transformation to 192 scenarios that vary dating intensity, search horizon, fit, and first-date conversion. The resulting index also incorporates the share of women ages 35-39 who have never married and the inflow rate of adults ages 25-34. Among 320 counties with complete data, the District of Columbia ranks first and New York County second under the baseline specification, and rankings remain highly stable under alternative component weights. An endogenous mobility extension shows that favorable markets attract additional male participants, producing substantial adjustment while leaving the top composite rankings relatively stable over the parameter values considered. The framework is intended as a structural comparison of local partner-market conditions rather than a predictor of individual relationship outcomes.

title: Machine Learning Models Trained on a Longitudinal Survey Dataset Poorly Predict Hundreds of Life Outcomes
abstract: Understanding the predictability of life outcomes is important for public policy and science, but existing studies focus on a limited number of outcomes and therefore struggle to describe the broad patterns of predictability. We developed a high-throughput approach that uses a single dataset to study the predictability of many future outcomes using past data. We deployed this approach with hundreds of outcomes and thousands of machine learning models per outcome in the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study. Three findings emerged. First, most outcomes were not very predictable, but some were much more predictable than others. Second, even for the most predictable outcomes, our complex prediction procedure typically exhibited little skill relative to a simple procedure. Third, we found modest patterns in how predictability varied across outcomes. We conclude by discussing scope conditions and how future research might address them.

title: Dynamic Panel Multinomial Logit Models
abstract: This paper provides moment conditions for dynamic multinomial logit panel data models with individual specific fixed effects. The moment conditions do not depend on the fixed effects and thus form the basis for generalized method of moments estimation. For a leading case, we provide sufficient conditions under which the moment conditions identify the common parameters, and we illustrate their use in an empirical application to household soft drink purchases. The construction of moment conditions is based on transformed models obtained by permuting outcomes across time periods. For any cyclic permutation, the ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability is free of the fixed effects, and comparing two such ratios yields restrictions on the common parameters of interest. This construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. It applies to any dynamic panel data model whose static counterpart admits a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. This unifies our main result with analogous results for other models.

title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.

title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
abstract: This paper develops a mathematical framework connecting structural metadata, logical admissibility, and correction in statistical data editing. A normalized routing graph generates a canonical indexed representation and an associated Horn theory, incorporating explicit semantic edits through deterministically evaluated auxiliary variables. Under specified record semantics, the theory characterizes admissibility, distinguishes structural minimality from logical irredundancy, and permits validation without materializing the deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the provenance and dependency scopes of violations. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible corrections within the permitted candidate domain. Verified zero-energy outputs therefore certify feasibility and global minimization of violation energy. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates obtained by matching attained costs with valid lower bounds. A household survey application verifies admissible corrections and certifies minimum cost for a subset of returned records through a retrospective audit. The framework connects structural requirements to correction certificates independently of the numerical search procedure, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

title: Online Fair Division with Upgrade Recourse
abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible goods. In the standard model, where assignments are irrevocable, no algorithm can guarantee any positive fraction of the maximin share (MMS). Reassigning earlier goods can restore fairness, but it may take value away from agents who already hold them. We ask how much fairness can be maintained if every reassignment must leave each affected agent at least as well off. We consider two forms of such upgrade recourse. Under item-level upgrades, each good an agent holds must be kept or replaced by a distinct good she values at least as much; under bundle-level upgrades, only her total value must not decrease. For item-level upgrades, we show that the optimal MMS factor is essentially $1/H_n \approx 1/\ln n$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and that fixed picking sequences nearly attain it. Since these sequences use only the agents' rankings of individual goods, knowing the actual values cannot improve the optimal factor for up to 33 agents, and improves it by at most a vanishing margin as $n$ grows. Bundle-level upgrades allow substantially stronger guarantees. By permitting several-for-one exchanges, they turn this vanishing factor into a constant: we achieve exact MMS for two agents and more than half of MMS for any number of agents, in both cases together with relaxations of envy-freeness. Finally, we show that predictions about future goods let online algorithms inherit any offline MMS guarantee, losing only an additive term bounded by the prediction error. Under item-level upgrades, however, insisting on exact MMS when predictions are correct leaves no positive guarantee when they are wrong.

title: A Composite Bayesian Risk--Distributionally Robust Optimization Model for Stochastic Programming with Elliptical Distribution Ambiguity
abstract: We study a stochastic optimization problem in which the random vector follows a semiparametric elliptical distribution with unknown location and shape parameters and an unspecified radial distribution. Assuming that the decision maker only has access to samples of the random vector, we develop a framework to jointly address parameter uncertainty and distributional ambiguity arising from this composite structure. To update the posterior distribution of the parameters, a key challenge is that the density of an elliptical distribution depends on the unknown radial distribution, and hence conventional likelihood-based Bayesian inference is infeasible. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel estimating-equation-based Gibbs inference framework that updates posterior distributions of model parameters solely through estimating equations. For elliptical distributions, we construct a pair of estimating equations for the location and shape parameters that are invariant to the radial component, which enables posterior learning without specifying the density. For the distributional uncertainty, we construct an ambiguity set for the radial distribution by transforming observed samples into pseudo-samples of the radial variable. Combining the above components, we formulate a composite Bayesian risk--distributionally robust optimization model, in which the inner problem captures worst-case radial distributions within the ambiguity set, and the outer problem evaluates the decision risk induced by the parameter uncertainty through a user-specified risk measure. We further develop a cutting-plane algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach provides substantial performance improvements over benchmark methods, including sample average approximation and distributionally robust optimization.

title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
abstract: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.

title: The Complexity of Exact and Approximate Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games
abstract: We prove that, for every fixed rational $c>0$, computing a $2^{-n^c}$-approximate Nash equilibrium in an $n$-player two-strategy anonymous game is $\mathsf{PPAD}$-complete. This holds even when one strategy always pays $1/2$ and, for all but two players, the other is constant outside at most five opponent counts. The reduction uses coefficient estimates to simulate circuit constraints approximately. Exact computation requires eliminating the simulation error: with three strategies, a separate construction uses polynomial roots to implement circuit gates exactly. This yields $\mathsf{FIXP}$-completeness of exact equilibrium computation under separable-linear reductions and $\mathsf{FIXP}_a$-completeness of approximation in distance to an exact equilibrium.

title: Adaptive Cauchy inference from invariant information
abstract: Selecting weights and projection directions from the observations used for testing can invalidate a reference distribution. We develop a framework for exact conditional inference under rotation symmetry. A maximal invariant permits adaptation while leaving a uniform common phase for calibration. This yields explicit Cauchy references for invariantly selected weights and projections. Under separate block rotations, the same principle gives exact normal-score combinations with coefficients selected from all blockwise invariants. The calibration results require neither densities nor moments. To illustrate the framework, we study direction learning and power in spherical Gaussian location models, identifying a regime in which consistent detection is possible without consistent direction recovery. For heterogeneous functional data, a matched mean--residual construction produces the required null symmetry under a conditional Gaussian model. Simulations compare Radius and Blend, two representative procedures, with sample splitting, and an electrocardiogram analysis illustrates their application.

title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
abstract: Next-generation wireless networks are expected to support high data rates and reliable connectivity while meeting requirements for energy efficiency, resource management, and communication security. Digital Twin (DT) technology represents expected network behavior and enables the actual network state to be assessed against it. Integrating DT technology with reinforcement learning (RL) supports adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) method for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network model. Receiver-level residuals between attack-free and attacked configurations are combined with candidate spatial jamming footprints and accumulated into a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into its state, reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. Compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs per configuration, with known jammer counts, BGQL achieves link-rate scores of 437.4-564.2 Mbit/s, rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37-76.79 Mbit/J, and localization recall of 100% for one jammer and 78%-81% for two jammers. BGQL requires 80-130 s per run versus 5-14 s for SARSA. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

title: Pseudo-Panel Event Studies: Econometric Foundations for Credible Applications
abstract: Event studies with panel data are widely used to estimate treatment effects. With repeated cross-sections, future treatment dates are unobserved for untreated individuals. Pseudo-panel event studies impute pre-treatment outcomes of the treated using matched untreated individuals. This paper establishes identification in such designs and characterizes bias when identification conditions fail. I show that the pseudo-panel regression is equivalent to weighted least squares with group means. This representation simplifies computation and yields analytical inference. In simulations, analytical confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage, whereas conventional intervals substantially undercover. I also develop a doubly robust estimator using richer covariates, a symmetric matching design with synthetic type fixed effects, and a fully nonparametric estimator that accommodates heterogeneous treatment effects. In a Korean panel survey, the pseudo-panel regression yields an employment child penalty of 42.1%, close to 46.9% in the actual panel. Applications to repeated cross-sections yield employment penalties of about one-third.

title: Quantifying Precision in Measurement of Individualized, Evidence-Based Learning Across Sessions in Applied Behavior Analysis Therapy
abstract: Current performance criteria used in Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) are often based on whether a learner meets a predetermined benchmark e.g., 8 out of 10 correct responses across several sessions. Although these criteria help practitioners make instructional decisions, they provide limited information about how likely it is that the learner has truly acquired the skill. In this paper, we introduce a Bayesian approach that combines practitioners' prior expectations with the learner's ongoing performance data to estimate the learner's future performance level. Rather than providing only a pass or fail decision based on the criteria, we add an element of precision around that criteria to make decisions more nuanced to the testing conditions used. We also developed an R Shiny application for Measurement of Individualized, Evidence-Based Learning (MIEBL) that allows practitioners to apply this method in practice, supporting more informed instructional decisions and providing insight into the strengths and limitations of commonly used mastery criteria.

title: Bounding MrP: Subnational public opinion estimation without detailed census data
abstract: Multilevel regression with post-stratification (MrP) is the dominant method for estimating public opinion in subnational units. The method requires the full joint distribution of demographic variables in a subnational unit, which is often unavailable from public census tabulations. Existing approaches fill this gap by imposing assumptions to combine marginal distributions of census variables into a synthetic joint distribution. We propose sharp MrP bounds instead: the smallest interval containing all estimates of subnational public opinion consistent with the marginal distributions alone. The bounds solve a pair of linear programs and are computationally feasible for typical applications in political science. Applied to two prominent examples in the literature, the bounds are tight enough to be informative and often more accurate than MrP restricted to a coarser, observed joint distribution of census variables. The bounds serve as margin-consistent interval estimates and a diagnostic when researchers use a synthetic joint distribution to construct MrP estimates.

title: Estimation of Rational Inattention--Additive Random Utility Models
abstract: This paper develops likelihood-based estimation for parametric rational inattention--additive random utility models. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the exact maximum likelihood estimator and provide conditions under which the simulated estimator shares its asymptotic distribution. To implement estimation, we develop Newton--BA, a KKT-guided hybrid of Newton--Raphson and Blahut--Arimoto (BA). The algorithm accommodates both interior and boundary solutions and substantially improves computational efficiency relative to direct BA while preserving numerical accuracy. Monte Carlo simulations show that parameter recovery improves with sample size and that confidence-interval coverage is generally close to the nominal $95$ percent level. Finally, we compare our model with no- and perfect-information logit benchmarks in an empirically calibrated ModeCanada experiment. Our model achieves similar in-sample likelihood fit to perfect-information logit but more accurately recovers key preference parameters, choice probabilities, and responses to travel-time changes.

title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
abstract: We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$. We show the following: - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability. - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $\mu = \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-\delta)\mu$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-\delta^2\mu/(2(\Delta^2+1)))$ for every $0\leq\delta\leq1$. -If $G$ has maximum degree $\Delta$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,\Delta^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.

title: Quickest Change-point Detection in Generalized Linear Models with Variational Estimation
abstract: We consider quickest change-point detection in generalized linear models when the post-change parameter is unknown. Such problems arise, for example, when monitoring whether the relationship between a learned representation and an observed response changes over time. Since detection must occur soon after a change, the post-change parameter must be estimated from a limited number of observations, making finite-sample estimation accuracy particularly important. We propose a window-limited CUSUM procedure that estimates the post-change parameter using a variational-inequality (VI) formulation. For noncanonical links, VI estimation can offer favorable finite-sample accuracy over short windows despite the asymptotic efficiency advantage of maximum likelihood estimation. We characterize how estimation error reduces the effective post-change information rate and affects detection delay, and derive finite-window guarantees accounting for both statistical error and incomplete numerical optimization. The resulting procedure retains false-alarm control and achieves first-order asymptotic optimality under suitable conditions. Numerical experiments compare detection delay and update cost for fixed-budget estimation and benchmark VI-WLCUSUM against alternative detectors.

title: Locally adaptive step sizes for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods
authors: Tore Selland Kleppe and Nawaf Bou-Rabee
abstract: Exact reversible locally adaptive step sizes are introduced by Bou-Rabee et al. (2026) in the context of the No-U-Turn Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampler for the purpose of high performance HMC sampling in challenging target distributions. This paper carefully explains and illustrates the locally adaptive step size procedure under more general assumptions. Alternative error measures are introduced with the aim of further enhancing MCMC performance by reducing the prevalence of reversibility failure rejections. In addition, the paper shows how to introduce the locally adaptive step sizes also within standard HMC and Metropolis-corrected kinetic Langevin/generalized HMC (GHMC). Finally, a numerical study of the relative merits of the proposed error measures in the context of different Hamiltonian flow-based MCMC methods is provided.

title: Honest Inference for High-Dimensional Linear Models
abstract: We propose a heteroskedasticity-robust and dimention-adaptive test for multiple linear restric- tions in sparse high-dimensional linear regression models. It combines desparsified LASSO estimation with a ridge-regularized quadratic form statistic and critical values that adapt to the restriction dimension. Under stated regularity conditions, our approach is asymptotically valid under a fixed or diverging number of restrictions without specifying the asymptotic regime in advance. Our random-design theory allows independent non-identically distributed covari- ate rows with marginal sub-Weibull tails and heteroskedastic errors satisfying finite polynomial moments. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate improved finite-sample size control relative to conventional Wald tests, particularly as the number of restrictions increases.

title: Some complete $\omega$-powers of a one-counter language in the difference hierarchy
abstract: Fix a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters, and natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$. We denote by $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of differences of $n$ subsets of the Cantor space $\Sigma^\omega$ in $\mathbf{\Pi}0_k$, and by $D_n-(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$ the class of complements of sets in $D_n(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$. We prove, for any natural numbers $n,k\geq 1$, the existence of a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ having at least two letters and a finitary language $U_{n,k}$ over $\Sigma$ accepted by a one-counter automaton such that the $\omega$-power $$U_{n,k}^\infty:={ w_0w_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\mid\forall i\in\omega ~~w_i\in U_{n,k}}$$ is $D_{2n-1}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. We also prove a conditional result for the dual classes $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$: under the assumption that there exists a finitary language $V_{n,3}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,3}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_3)$-complete, there would also exist, for any integer $k>3$, a finitary language $V_{n,k}$ accepted by a one-counter automaton, such that its $\omega$-power $V_{n,k}^\infty$ is $D^-_{2n}(\mathbf{\Pi}^0_k)$-complete. Finally we add another conditionnal result about Wadge degrees of rational $\mathbf{\Delta}^0_2$ omega powers, which completes the recent results of [FGL26].

title: Online Individualized Treatment Selection under Partial Feedback: False Discovery Control and Minimax Optimality
abstract: We study online individualized treatment selection when only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed. Our objective is to preferentially treat individuals whose potential outcomes under treatment exceed a covariate-specific control reference, while limiting false discoveries among treated individuals. We propose Partial-Feedback Adaptive Individualized Treatment Selection (PAITS), which initializes learning from historical data and combines sequential estimation of local null risks, randomized exploration, and feedback-driven updates of the treatment selection threshold. Under regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control and sublinear gap-weighted assignment regret relative to a population oracle. We further establish a minimax lower bound on assignment regret under prescribed uniform nuisance-estimation requirements and give conditions under which PAITS attains the corresponding constrained minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. These results quantify the tradeoff between accurate treatment assignment and nuisance learning under partial feedback. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis using the Jester recommendation dataset illustrate the finite-sample performance of PAITS.

title: Measuring intraday return-shape geometry with modified Brownian motion
abstract: Realised kurtosis measures intraday tail risk but compresses the shape of the return distribution into a single scalar, so trading days with similar kurtosis may differ in how probability mass is spread across the peak, the shoulders and the tails. We propose a geometric description of intraday return shape based on the modified Brownian motion model (MBMM), which deforms a Gaussian benchmark through a nonlinear feedback governed by a shape parameter and a distortion intensity. Our main contribution is a peak-shoulder-tail decomposition that measures where the fitted return density gains or loses probability mass relative to the Gaussian, complemented by two feedback landmarks that explain how the shape parameter generates these deformations. We estimate the model at the stock-day level using a bin-free simulation-based minimum-distance estimator that matches empirical and model-implied intraday quantiles, and we document its finite-sample reliability by Monte Carlo. Using regular session one-minute returns for ten liquid U.S. stocks from May 2021 to April 2026, we find that the MBMM provides a substantially better in-sample fit than geometric Brownian motion on every estimator-ready stock-day, and that days with closely matched realised kurtosis can display materially different peak-shoulder-tail geometries. Finally, we show that the estimated shape parameters behave as persistent daily state variables: they are strongly forecastable relative to a random-walk benchmark, though their predictability reflects persistence around a slowly moving level rather than rich autoregressive dynamics. The proposed decomposition offers a risk-shape measurement layer that complements realised kurtosis by describing not only how large intraday tail risk is, but how it is formed, giving investors and risk managers additional distributional information for risk monitoring and, potentially, prediction.

title: Enhancing Statistical-Computational Balance in Uncertainty Quantification of Bagging: A Cheap Bootstrap Approach
abstract: Bagging, which refers to the repeated subsampling of data and averaging the resulting outputs, is a common approach to reduce sampling variability of unstable learning and data-driven optimization procedures. However, uncertainty quantification for these bagged estimators, namely to generate confidence intervals for their target quantities, faces challenges in the simultaneous attainment of coverage validity while being computationally affordable. The latter refers to the practical consideration of overall resampling effort which, when using conventional bootstraps for instance, would lead to nested resampling procedures and thus can be multiplicatively large. In this paper, we develop an interval construction approach that is both asymptotically coverage-valid and computationally light in that it does not use much more than the resampling effort in the bagging scheme itself. Our approach builds on the recent so-called cheap bootstrap idea, a method designed to substantially reduce the number of resamples based on an integrative treatment between data noises and Monte Carlo resampling noises, and an in-depth derivation of the algorithmic configurations under which the Monte Carlo error from incomplete bagging is negligible. Our theory shows that our required computation budget is significantly smaller than existing methods in relation to the bag size and number of Monte Carlo subsamples. Numerical experiments in random forests, as well as an optimality bound estimation in stochastic optimization where bagging is useful, show that our proposed intervals achieve reliable coverage with low computation cost.

title: When Sample-Splitting Choices Matter in TMLE and AIPW: Cross-Fitting, Targeting, and Repetition
abstract: Variants of targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with machine-learning nuisance models differ in which observations train them, how bias is corrected, and whether splits are repeated. In known-truth simulations of a binary-outcome average treatment effect, eight headline estimators shared each setting's library, inner folds and truncation bound; coverage differences were judged against a prespecified two-percentage-point margin. With a low-complexity library and good overlap (n = 3000), all but a half-sample baseline covered equivalently (0.928-0.939). With one random forest on the primary data-generating mechanism, estimators fitting the propensity in-sample undercovered severely (0.12-0.48), whereas cross-fitting both nuisances raised coverage to 0.91-1.00, two overcovering. Under near-positivity, every AIPW estimator covered better than every TMLE estimator with the unweighted fluctuation (0.907-0.917 versus 0.656-0.806 at the primary setting, all undercovering); looser truncation widened the gap. At the primary settings, pooled-versus-fold-specific and single-versus-double cross-fit constructions (involving four additional estimators) were usually equivalent; under extreme weights, pooled-targeting estimates were 1.7-1.8 times as dispersed as fold-specific ones. Repetition reduced partition dependence but made several intervals more conservative. Two real-data analyses illustrate these sensitivities. Results support cross-fitting both nuisances when empirical-process conditions cannot be justified, and assessing truncation and AIPW-versus-TMLE sensitivity under poor overlap.

title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.
